source.title: Scaling Repeated-Data Pretraining: Batch Size, Regularization, and GPU-Time Tradeoffs

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper refines the scope of scaling claims for repeated-data pretraining: its results show dependence on batch size and training recipe, finite useful repetition horizons, and a fitted loss curve with both improvement and degradation terms.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses conventional scaling laws and cites earlier results, but those cited results are not recorded here. Its GPU-time and latency projections concern resource allocation rather than a tested parameter/token/compute-optimal split. Recorded results focus on its own repeated-data loss experiments, fits, and downstream evaluations.
record.test_reason: The repeated-data loss trajectories and their fitted improvement-plus-degradation curve bear on V5 and the curve-bending component of V7. Downstream evaluations bear on V6, with agreement depending on metric and training method. Batch-size and recipe endpoint comparisons alone do not test a power-law form.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: repeated-data pretraining requires jointly choosing batch size, repetitions, recipe, and GPU/time allocation. Smaller batches improve the unconstrained frontier; repacking and embedding regularization extend useful training; shorter deadlines can favor larger batches. The 70B/10T resource estimate is explicitly illustrative and unvalidated.
record.recipe_differences: This is an empirical study of repeated-data pretraining rather than a reproduction of the original single-pass scaling-law experiments. It measures validation loss across batch sizes, recipes, model sizes, data pools, and repetition horizons.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with batch size, data-loader policy, embedding tying and embedding decay, model size, unique-data-pool size, training horizon, and deadline/GPU budget.

fits_no_version.finding: Batch size has an interior optimum, and loader and embedding regularization change attainable loss and useful repetition horizons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Repeated-data loss frontiers depend on batch size and training recipe.

fits_no_version.finding: Power functions summarize fitted practical stopping epochs and selected batch sizes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stopping horizons and preferred batches may admit empirical scaling relationships in repeated-data training.

record.code_released: Code and exact commands will be released upon acceptance.
record.problems: The measured models are limited to 153M–1.5B parameters and data pools to 0.333B–3B tokens. The 70B/10T resource estimate is an extreme extrapolation without target-scale statistical validation. The paper notes possible dependence on dense architecture, AdamW with WSD, context length, and the filtered DCLM-Baseline corpus. The batch-size fit has log-space R²=0.768 and is described by the authors as unreliable; downstream curves show greater variance than validation loss.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed per-epoch checkpoint curves in Figures 3–5, further original-versus-repetition-aware comparisons, and GPU-time frontier cells in Figures 8–9 are not listed separately; they add many checkpoint or resource-budget measurements but do not directly test the claim's parameter/token/compute power laws or compute-optimal parameter/token split. The simulated latency projections in Appendix D.2 are not end-to-end measurements.

untested.parts: Unbottlenecked pretraining-loss power laws over several orders of magnitude.
Prediction and empirical validation of loss on runs orders of magnitude larger; the 70B/10T projection is unvalidated.
Loss-minimizing parameter/token allocation at fixed compute and its scaling exponents.
Architecture variation at fixed parameter count; tying changes parameter count.
Other modalities, fine-tuning, transfer, and generalization beyond the measured repeated-data text regime.
Calibrated quantitative downstream predictions across orders of magnitude in model size or compute.

Sensitivity of published scaling exponents and compute-optimal parameter/token splits to alternative counting, schedules, datasets, or fitting procedures. Only departure from a single power-law trajectory is directly tested.

missing.what: Matched-step DiLoCo comparisons dissociate downstream accuracy from validation CE. At 2,861 steps, CE worsens from 3.160 to 3.170 while HellaSwag accuracy increases from 37.64% to 40.72%; at 5,722 steps, DiLoCo CE is 3.128 versus baseline values 3.091 and 3.122, while accuracy is 45.81% versus 40.71% and 43.20%. These comparisons are not declared in rows_left_out.

record.verdict_notes: Nominal size labels are retained by the paper after tying, but scaling fits use actual tied counts. The U-shaped batch sweep is not itself evidence against parameter/token/compute power laws. No verdict is based on the unvalidated large-scale resource extrapolation.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test held-out loss as a power law in parameter count, tokens, or compute when the other quantities are not bottlenecks.
It extrapolates a fitted stopping epoch and batch size, not validation loss of larger runs; no target-scale run validates those predictions.
It does not find the loss-minimizing parameter/token allocation at fixed training compute.
Architecture details are described, but depth, width, or other architecture choices are not varied to test their effect on loss.
Only repeated-data text pretraining is studied; other modalities, fine-tuning, transfer, and other training regimes are not tested.
Downstream metrics are evaluated across batches and checkpoints, but the paper does not establish a general quantitative mapping from pretraining loss or scale to downstream performance.

The paper varies training setup and fits repeated-data-specific curves, but does not compare published scaling-law exponents or test how alternative fitting choices change the conventional compute-optimal split.
